title: what
parentNote: One word today, learned whole: what. The wh at the front is honest — it says wuh, the same as it did yesterday — and the t on the end is honest too. It is the a that lies: it says o, so the word is wot, not the rhyme-with-hat your child will reach for first. There is a reason worth telling them, because it is a pattern and not a one-off: a w in front of an a bends it into an o nearly every time, which is why we say wot and swop and wosh. Today also changes what this course can ask. Every comprehension question so far has had to be a sentence with the end left off — the fox did sit next to dot dot dot — because what and who and where were all unreadable, and you cannot ask a question without a question word. From today we can ask a real one, and the story below ends with three of them. If your child has been answering by pattern rather than by thinking, this is the week you will notice.

activities.sentence: "What is in that box?" said Meg, and I did not want to tell her.
activities.prompt: Do not sound this one out. It looks like it should rhyme with hat. It says wot.
No sounding out. Look at it and say it: what.
This is the sound in the middle of what. Find it.
Now find the letter that is really sitting in the middle of what. It is doing somebody else's job in that word, and the w next to it is what bends it.
No new sound today, so all of these are words you can already sound out.
The long one. Two short words stuck together, and each one has a team in it.
Three words that start with a wuh. Two of them you sound out and one of them you just know.
All three are tiny. Listen to the front of the word, and then right to the end.
This one is hard. All three start with a wuh. Everything you need is the sound in the middle.

activities.text: "What is that up in the oak?" said Meg, and I said it is a hawk.
I did ask Dad what time we can go, and he said we can go at six.
Mum said, "What do you want on it?" and I said all the jam.
What did you do with my red kite? It is not in the shed.

activities.title: What is in the shed?
activities.prompt: This story ends with a real question. Read it, then go back and hunt for the bit that tells you.
lines: At sun up, a thing in the shed did go bump. Then it did bump a bit more.
"What is that?" said Meg, and she did grab my hand.
Dad said, "It is a rat," but Mum said rats do not bump like that.
So we did all stand up at the shed, and we did not go in.
Meg said, "What can we do?" and I said we can peep in at the gap.
In the dark I did see a big white thing lift and drop and lift and drop.
"It is tall!" I said. "It is the tallest thing in the shed!"
Dad did get a lamp, and then we did all go in at the same time.
The big white thing is a sheet, and it did land on the fan.
The fan did lift it up and drop it, lift it and drop it, all on its own.
"That is my sheet!" said Meg. "Why is it out in the shed?"
Dad did go red. "I did want to dry it in the sun," he said, "and then I did not."

questions.prompt: What did we see lift and drop in the dark?
What did the sheet land on?
Why is the sheet out in the shed?
choices: Dad did want to dry it in the sun
Meg did drop it in the shed
The rat did drag it in
questions.answer: Dad did want to dry it in the sun
